objectives: Describe the functions and hierarchy of settlements
Explain urban land-use models and apply them to African cities
reviewNotes: Statements about Douala and Yaoundé are limited to well-known roles; check any case-study details.

blocks.title: Hierarchy and services
blocks.md: Settlements form a **hierarchy**: many hamlets and villages, fewer towns, very few large cities. Services with a high **threshold** (minimum customers needed) and long **range** (distance people will travel) such as hospitals and universities occur in larger centres; corner shops occur everywhere. This is the basis of **central place theory**.

blocks.title: Land-use models
blocks.md: The **concentric zone** model has a Central Business District (CBD), an inner zone, then suburbs. The **sector** model shows wedges of land use along transport routes. African cities often depart from the models: colonial planning, a port or river site, traditional neighbourhoods and **informal settlements** on the margins or low land. Douala is the main port and economic city; Yaoundé is the political capital.

blocks.caption: The concentric zone model of a city (simplified).
blocks.alt: Three concentric circles labelled CBD, inner zone and suburbs.

blocks.title: Planning
blocks.md: Challenges: housing, water, sanitation, transport, waste, floods, jobs. Responses: land-use planning and zoning, **site and service** schemes, slum upgrading with community involvement, mass transport, green spaces, drainage, and decentralised growth to secondary towns. A **sustainable city** meets present needs without harming future generations.

blocks.title: Avoid these errors
blocks.md:
- Models are simplifications: real cities do not match them exactly.
- Informal settlements are home to workers the city depends on; evictions without alternatives create new problems.
- Capital city and economic capital are not always the same.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Threshold and range
blocks.statement: Why is there a hospital in the regional town but only a clinic in a village?
steps: A hospital needs a large population (high threshold) to stay open.
People will travel a long way for a hospital (long range).
A village does not have the threshold, so it has a clinic with a smaller catchment.
blocks.answer: Higher-order services need larger thresholds and are in larger centres.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Apply the model
blocks.statement: Describe how the concentric model may not fit a port city growing along a river.
steps: Growth follows the river, port and main roads, not equal rings.
Low or flood-prone land attracts informal housing.
Industry stretches along the port and railway.
blocks.answer: Site, transport and informal growth distort the pattern.

blocks.title: Industrial location
blocks.md: Industries locate by balancing **raw materials, power, market, transport, labour, capital** and **government policy**. Agro-processing (cocoa, cotton, palm oil, timber), brewing, cement, aluminium, oil refining and small informal industries are common in Cameroon, with Douala as the main industrial centre because of its port, market and labour.

blocks.title: Examples
blocks.md: An aluminium smelter at Edéa uses hydroelectricity from the Sanaga river. An oil refinery operates at Limbe. Plantation agriculture around Mount Cameroon supplies processing plants. Challenges: unreliable power supply, high transport costs, small domestic markets, competition from imports, shortage of skilled workers and credit. Policies include industrial zones, incentives and regional trade.

blocks.caption: Factors that influence the location of industry.
blocks.alt: Six boxes naming raw materials, power, market, transport, labour and capital and policy.

blocks.title: Energy
blocks.md: **Non-renewable:** oil, gas, coal. **Renewable:** hydropower, solar, wind, biomass, geothermal. Hydroelectricity supplies a major part of Cameroon’s electricity but varies with rainfall; many households rely on **fuelwood and charcoal**, which adds to forest loss. Solar power has large potential in the sunny north. Rural electrification and efficient cooking are development priorities.

blocks.title: Do not say
blocks.md:
- That ‘renewable’ means ‘free of impact’: dams have social and environmental costs.
- That industry always locates near raw materials: weight-gaining products locate near the market.
- Use of precise energy statistics: use only qualitative statements unless you can cite a source.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Location of an aluminium smelter
blocks.statement: Explain why an aluminium smelter may be located near a large hydroelectric power station.
steps: Smelting uses very large amounts of electricity.
Cheap, reliable power cuts costs.
A port nearby helps import raw material and export the product.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Fuelwood and forests
blocks.statement: Explain why dependence on fuelwood is an environmental problem.
steps: Many households cook with wood or charcoal.
Cutting trees near towns causes deforestation and erosion.
Smoke indoors harms health, so cleaner stoves and fuels help.
blocks.answer: Fuelwood use contributes to deforestation and health risks.

blocks.title: Development indicators
blocks.md: Economic: **GDP per capita**. Social: life expectancy, literacy, infant mortality, access to clean water. The **Human Development Index (HDI)** combines income, health and education. Averages hide inequality inside countries; a mix of indicators gives the clearest picture.

blocks.title: Terms of trade
blocks.md: $\text{Terms of trade} = \frac{\text{export price index}}{\text{import price index}} \times 100$. A value below 100 means export prices have fallen relative to import prices: the country can buy fewer imports for the same exports.

blocks.caption: Illustrative price indices: year 1 equal, year 2 export prices fall and import prices rise.
blocks.alt: Four bars: export and import price indices for two years; the exports bar falls to 80 and imports rise to 120.

blocks.title: Trade and cooperation
blocks.md: Many African economies depend on **primary products** (oil, cocoa, coffee, timber, cotton, minerals) whose prices fluctuate, while manufactured imports cost more. **Aid** may be bilateral, multilateral or from NGOs; **debt** repayments can limit spending. Regional blocs aim to increase trade and cooperation: CEMAC (Central Africa, which includes Cameroon), ECOWAS (West Africa) and the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA, agreed in 2018).

blocks.title: Avoid these errors
blocks.md:
- Do not equate GDP per capita with how well off everybody is.
- A fall in terms of trade is NOT a fall in the quantity of exports.
- Aid can help but may create dependency or be tied to conditions.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Terms of trade
blocks.statement: Export price index = 80; import price index = 120. Calculate the terms of trade and interpret.
steps: Below 100: the country can now buy only about two-thirds of the imports it could buy before for the same exports.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Why diversify?
blocks.statement: Explain why dependence on one export crop is risky.
steps: World prices change with supply and demand, so income is unstable.
A pest or drought can destroy the crop.
Diversification into processing and several products spreads the risk.
blocks.answer: Income instability and lack of resilience.

lessons.title: Rural settlement and tourism
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board, Advanced Level Geography syllabus (Upper Sixth) — to be checked against the official text

lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Classify rural settlement patterns and explain their causes
Describe tourist attractions and the impacts of tourism in Cameroon
reviewNotes: Settlement patterns in Cameroon are generalisations; confirm with the teacher’s local case studies.
Names of attractions (Mount Cameroon, Limbe, Kribi, Waza, Foumban) are well known; check current status and access.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Settlement patterns
blocks.md: **Nucleated** settlements have buildings clustered around a centre (a village square, spring, chief’s compound); **dispersed** settlements have scattered farms or compounds; **linear** settlements stretch along a road, river or valley. **Site** is the exact location; **situation** its position relative to surroundings. Factors: water supply, defence, relief and drainage, soils, routes, land tenure and history.

blocks.title: Patterns in Cameroon
blocks.md: In forest regions, villages often line the roads (linear), partly because roads were built to link them. In the western highlands compounds are often dispersed among farms. In the savanna and Sahel, clusters near water, such as wells and rivers, are common. These are general patterns, with many exceptions.

blocks.caption: Three rural settlement patterns.
blocks.alt: Dots clustered together for nucleated, dots scattered for dispersed and dots in a row along a line for linear.

blocks.title: Tourism
blocks.md: Attractions include Mount Cameroon, the beaches of Limbe and Kribi, waterfalls, national parks and reserves such as Waza in the north, cultural heritage in places like Foumban, and festivals. **Benefits:** jobs, income, infrastructure, conservation funding. **Costs:** pollution, pressure on land and water, cultural change, benefits leaking abroad, seasonal work. **Ecotourism** aims to conserve nature and benefit local people. Constraints: infrastructure, marketing, security perceptions and cost of travel.

blocks.title: Evaluation tip
blocks.md: In tourism questions give both benefits and costs, name a place, and show who gains and who loses. Avoid sweeping statements like ‘tourism always brings development’.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Explain a linear village
blocks.statement: Why might a forest village stretch along a road?
steps: The road brings access to markets and services.
Homes near the road are convenient for trading and travel.
Farmland lies behind the houses on each side.
blocks.answer: Access to the road gives a line of houses.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Impacts of tourism
blocks.statement: Give one benefit and one cost of tourism at a national park, with who is affected.
steps: Benefit: guides and lodge workers from nearby villages earn income.
Cost: more vehicles and waste may disturb animals and ecosystems.
A fair share of fees can help local people accept conservation.
blocks.answer: Income for locals but environmental pressure; management is needed.
